cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: Audience theories attempt to explain the relationship between media products and audiences — how media affects people and how people use media.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: Hypodermic needle model (1920s-1930s): media injects ideas directly into passive audiences, who are uniformly affected. Now largely discredited but still influences public concern about media effects.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: Two-step flow model (Katz and Lazarsfeld, 1955): media messages pass through opinion leaders (influential people) who interpret and pass them on to wider audiences. More nuanced than the hypodermic model.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: Uses and Gratifications theory (Blumler and Katz, 1974): audiences actively choose media to fulfil four needs — information/education, entertainment, social interaction, and personal identity.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: Reception theory (Stuart Hall, 1980): audiences decode media texts in three ways — preferred reading (accepting the intended meaning), negotiated reading (partially accepting), and oppositional reading (rejecting).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: Cultivation theory (Gerbner): long-term exposure to media gradually shapes perceptions of reality — e.g. heavy TV viewers overestimate the amount of violence in society (the 'mean world syndrome').

cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: Media effects debate: does media cause behaviour change? Evidence is contested — some studies find short-term effects (increased aggression after violent games), but causal links to real-world violence are weak.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: Moral panics about media effects recur throughout history: comic books, rock music, video nasties, video games, and social media have all been blamed for social problems.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: Active audience theory has become dominant, but audiences are not always fully active — context, mood, and habit affect how critically we engage with media.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: The Frankfurt School (Adorno, Horkheimer) argued that the culture industry produces standardised content that pacifies audiences, preventing critical thinking — a pessimistic view of media effects.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: In the digital age, audiences have more power: they create content (prosumers), share opinions publicly, and can challenge producers. But algorithms and platform design also shape behaviour.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Audience Theories & Debates
cards.back: Media literacy: the ability to critically analyse media products and understand their construction. Media literacy empowers audiences to resist manipulation and engage actively.

cards.front: What should you know about media studies exam tips — audience theories & debates?
cards.back: 1. For Audience Theories & Debates, use media terminology precisely (e.g. connotation, denotation, representation, ideology) 2. Always analyse how media language creates meaning for specific audiences 3. Reference specific examples from set products to support your analysis 4. When evaluating Audience Theories & Debates, consider the role of media industries and cultural contexts 5. For extended answers, debate different interpretations before reaching your own
